claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability of multi-element near-equiatomic nanoparticles is governed by nanoscale elemental homogeneity.
A uniform elemental distribution promotes high-entropy stabilization.
High-entropy stabilization impedes diffusion-driven phase separation.
The baseline nanoparticles initially have a homogeneous near-equiatomic elemental distribution.
Controlled pre-annealing can create slight compositional gradients in the nanoparticles.
The intervention produces a less homogeneous elemental distribution than the untreated baseline.
Surface and interfacial elemental ordering and distribution mediate nanoparticle stability.
A uniform elemental distribution retards diffusion-driven dealloying at high temperature.
Induced compositional heterogeneity reduces entropic stabilization.
Reduced entropic stabilization accelerates nanoparticle degradation.
Homogeneous baseline nanoparticles will retain structure and composition better than pre-annealed heterogeneous nanoparticles under the specified service conditions.
Pre-annealed nanoparticles with induced gradients will exhibit more phase separation than the homogeneous baseline.
Pre-annealed nanoparticles with induced gradients will exhibit more surface segregation than the homogeneous baseline.
Pre-annealed nanoparticles with induced gradients will lose more catalytic or thermoelectric performance than the homogeneous baseline.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply only to nearly equiatomic, nanometric systems within the specified temperature ranges.
Composition deviations, extreme particle-size variations, or temperatures well outside the specified ranges may cause alternative stability mechanisms to dominate.
